topics.title: Starting a project: problem, objectives and target group

learn.hook: Why do auto-rickshaws in your town overcharge at night? A good statistics project turns a question like this into data, findings and practical suggestions.
points: A project applies statistical tools to a real economic issue, studies it systematically and suggests improvements.
Step 1: identify the problem or area of study and set clear, specific objectives (what exactly do we want to find out?).
Step 2: choose the target group, i.e. the population whose members will be surveyed (e.g. auto drivers and commuters of a city, or households of a colony).
A precise objective decides what data are needed; a well-defined target group decides whom to ask and how to sample.

example.q: A student wants to study 'saving habits'. Turn this into a clear objective and target group.
steps: Specific objective: 'To find what share of monthly income households in Ward 12 save, and where they keep their savings.'
Target group: all households in Ward 12.
example.answer: Objective: share of income saved and savings instruments used; target group: households of Ward 12.

learn.reallife: Before launching a new metro line, planners first define the objective (reduce travel time) and target group (daily commuters on the corridor) before collecting any data.

games.title: Starting a project
items: Identify the target group to be surveyed

games.title: Clear or vague objective?
items: Find the average daily earnings of street vendors in Sector 5
Find what percentage of Class 11 students in our school use public transport
Compare milk prices charged above MRP in 20 shops of our market

quiz.q: The first step in a statistical project is to:
options: Identify the problem and set objectives
quiz.explain: Without a defined problem and objectives, the study has no direction.
quiz.mistake: Starts with data analysis before knowing what to study

quiz.q: The 'target group' in a project refers to:
options: The population whose members are to be surveyed
The examiners who grade the project
The sources listed in the bibliography
quiz.explain: It is the population relevant to the problem being studied.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the target group with the audience of the report

quiz.q: A student studies overcharging by bus conductors in her city. A suitable target group is:
options: All bus commuters and conductors on city routes
quiz.explain: Those who use or operate city buses are directly connected to the issue.
quiz.mistake: Picks a group unrelated to the problem

quiz.q: Which is the best objective for a project?
options: To study everything about the economy
To find the share of income spent on food by 100 households in our colony
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable and tied to a clear group.
quiz.mistake: Accepts a vague, unmeasurable objective

quiz.q: A project aims to apply statistical tools to an economic issue in order to:
options: Understand the issue and suggest improvements
quiz.explain: The goal is to study a problem systematically and suggest solutions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks projects are only about diagrams

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A clearly defined objective helps decide what data must be collected.
Reason (R): The objective states exactly what the study wants to find out.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Knowing exactly what we want to find tells us which data are needed.
quiz.mistake: Does not link objectives with data needs

quiz.q: A study of 'drinking water availability in Ward 7' has 1,200 households. If 10% are surveyed, how many households are in the sample?
quiz.mistake: Slips a decimal place

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the first two steps of a project?
quiz.explain: The bibliography comes at the very end of the report.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of steps

teach.ask: Gappu wants to do a project on 'why some birds have tiny nests'. 'Where do I even start?'
teach.praise: Tweet! First define the problem, then set clear objectives, then pick the target group. Project launched!
teach.nudge: Good start! But who exactly will you collect data from? And what precisely do you want to find out?

learn.hook: You have two weeks and no budget. Do you knock on 500 doors or use the NSS report in the library? Smart projects choose their data sources deliberately.
points: Step 3: collect data. Primary data come from a questionnaire or interview schedule, through personal interviews, post, phone or email. Secondary data come from published sources such as the Census, NSS reports or RBI publications.
Decide census or sample; if sampling, choose a sampling method (random sampling is preferred to avoid bias).
A mailed questionnaire should carry a covering letter explaining the purpose of the survey, assuring confidentiality, and requesting a reply by a date.
When time or money is short, suitable secondary data are a sensible choice, but check that they match your purpose and are reliable.

example.q: A student studying women's employment in her district has 10 days and no funds. How should she collect data?
steps: A full primary survey of the district is too costly and slow.
Use secondary data (e.g. Census and PLFS reports) for the district picture.
Add a small random sample of households in her locality for primary insight, using a short questionnaire.
example.answer: Mainly secondary data, supplemented by a small random sample survey.

learn.reallife: NGOs studying sanitation often combine Census data on toilets per household with a small sample survey of their own villages.

games.title: Data collection for projects
items: A covering letter should accompany a mailed questionnaire.
It explains the purpose and requests cooperation.
Secondary data never need to be checked.
They must be checked for suitability and reliability.
Random sampling helps avoid bias in a project survey.
Each unit gets an equal chance.
An interview schedule is filled in by the interviewer.
The interviewer asks and records the answers.
A covering letter should reveal respondents' answers to others.

quiz.q: A covering letter sent with a postal questionnaire mainly aims to:
options: Explain the purpose of the survey and request cooperation
quiz.explain: It introduces the survey, assures confidentiality and asks for a reply.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the role of a covering letter

quiz.q: A student has very little time and money for her project. The most practical source of data is:
options: A census of the whole state
quiz.explain: Published data save time and cost, if they suit the purpose.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary data are always required

quiz.q: Which method of primary data collection is most suitable when respondents are spread far apart and literate?
quiz.explain: It is cheap and covers a wide area.
quiz.mistake: Picks personal interviews regardless of cost

quiz.q: Out of 400 questionnaires mailed for a project, 100 were returned. What is the response rate?
quiz.mistake: Divides 400 by 100

quiz.q: An interview schedule differs from a questionnaire because it is:
options: Filled in by the interviewer while asking the questions
quiz.explain: The enumerator asks questions and records the answers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both are filled by the respondent

quiz.q: Why should a project use random sampling where possible?
options: To give every unit an equal chance and reduce bias
To avoid making a sampling frame
quiz.explain: Random selection makes the sample more representative.
quiz.mistake: Prefers convenience sampling

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Secondary data should be used with caution in a project.
Reason (R): They may have been collected for a different purpose or with different definitions.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Mismatched purpose or definitions can make secondary data unsuitable.
quiz.mistake: Trusts all published data automatically

quiz.q: Which is an example of secondary data a project on employment could use?
options: Interviews with workers in the student's colony
Notes from a pilot survey the student conducted
quiz.explain: PLFS reports are published by NSO, so they are secondary data for the student.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the student's own survey is secondary

teach.ask: Gappu must collect data for his nest project but has only a week. 'Should I survey every bird or use old forest records?'
teach.praise: Tweet! With little time and money, I'll use reliable records and a small random sample survey with a covering letter!
teach.nudge: Good! Think about time and cost. What are the two kinds of data you could use?

topics.title: Organising, analysing, concluding and the bibliography

learn.hook: A pile of 200 filled questionnaires is not a project. It becomes one only after it is tabulated, graphed, analysed and turned into clear conclusions.
points: Step 4: organise and present the data in tables and suitable diagrams (bar diagrams, pie diagrams, histograms).
Step 5: analyse and interpret using averages (mean, median, mode) and correlation. (The NCERT book also mentions measures of dispersion, which are not part of the current syllabus.)
Step 6: draw conclusions from the analysis, forecast future prospects if relevant, and suggest policies or improvements.
Step 7: prepare a bibliography listing every secondary source used (books, reports, websites) so that readers can check them.

example.q: A project finds that average monthly saving of 50 households is ₹4,500 and correlation between income and saving is 0.85. What conclusion and suggestion fit?
steps: Average saving of ₹4,500 summarises saving levels.
r = 0.85 means higher-income households tend to save more (strong positive correlation).
Suggestion: savings schemes could target lower-income families with small, regular deposit options.
example.answer: Saving rises strongly with income; suggest small-saving schemes for lower-income households.

learn.reallife: The Economic Survey ends many chapters with policy suggestions and lists its data sources, just like a well-written project report.

games.title: Match the step to its tool

quiz.q: Which step comes immediately after collecting data in a project?
quiz.explain: Raw data must first be organised and presented before analysis.
quiz.mistake: Jumps straight to conclusions

quiz.q: Which statistical tools are mainly used for analysis in a Class 11 project?
quiz.explain: Mean, median, mode and correlation help analyse the data.
quiz.mistake: Confuses presentation tools with analysis tools

quiz.q: A bibliography in a project report lists:
quiz.explain: It records books, reports and websites consulted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it lists respondents

quiz.q: A project on household spending finds food takes 45% of income. Which diagram best shows the full split of spending?
quiz.explain: Shares of a total are best shown as a pie diagram.
quiz.mistake: Uses a histogram for parts of a whole

quiz.q: A project finds r = −0.7 between price of vegetables and quantity bought per family. The correct interpretation is:
options: Families buy more when prices are higher
Families tend to buy less when prices are higher
quiz.explain: A fairly strong negative correlation means quantity bought tends to fall as price rises.
quiz.mistake: Misreads the sign of r

quiz.q: Which of the following belongs in the conclusion of a project report?
options: A raw list of all questionnaire answers
A list of respondents' phone numbers
quiz.explain: The conclusion summarises findings and gives suggestions.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the conclusion with an appendix

quiz.q: The mean monthly income of 40 sampled families is ₹25,000. What is the total income of the sample?
quiz.mistake: Divides instead of multiplying

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A project report should end with suggestions.
Reason (R): The purpose of a project is to study an issue and suggest ways to improve the situation.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Suggestions fulfil the project's aim of improving the situation studied.
quiz.mistake: Thinks projects stop at presenting data

teach.ask: Gappu has 200 filled survey forms on his desk. 'Now what? How do I turn them into a project report?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Organise into tables and diagrams, analyse with averages and correlation, conclude with suggestions, and list sources!
teach.nudge: Good! After making tables, how will you analyse them? And what goes at the very end?

topics.title: Project ideas: playing an economic role

learn.hook: Imagine you are the transport advisor to your district collector, or a bank officer judging a loan for a pickle-making unit. Projects are most fun when you play a role.
points: Transport advisor: study bus routes, waiting times and fares to suggest better services. Bank loan proposal: assess costs, sales and profits of a cottage unit. Advertising: study whether ad spending raises a firm's sales.

Literacy and dropouts: find why children leave school in a locality. Overcharging: check whether shops charge above MRP. Drinking water: survey availability and quality. Women's employment: study participation and wages.
Health and sanitation, food adulteration, immunisation coverage, household saving habits, and problems of farmers are other good areas.
Each role-based project still follows the same steps: problem, objectives, target group, data, presentation, analysis, conclusions, bibliography.

example.q: As a bank officer, what data would you need to judge a loan proposal for a cottage unit making papads?
steps: Costs: raw materials, labour, rent, machines.
Expected profit = revenue − cost, and ability to repay.
example.answer: Cost, sales, profit and repayment-capacity data.

learn.reallife: Many schools encourage CBSE projects on local issues, such as checking whether packaged water is sold above MRP at railway stations.

games.title: Match the role to the data needed

quiz.q: A student acting as 'transport advisor' to the collector would most need data on:
options: Bus routes, frequency, waiting times and fares
quiz.explain: These variables relate directly to improving public transport.
quiz.mistake: Picks data unrelated to the role

quiz.q: To study whether advertising increases sales, the most useful statistical tool is:
options: Pie diagram of colours used in ads
Correlation between ad spending and sales
quiz.explain: Correlation measures how ad spending and sales move together.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a tool that does not relate two variables

quiz.q: A papad-making unit's monthly costs are ₹40,000 and expected sales revenue is ₹55,000. What is its expected monthly profit?
quiz.explain: Profit = revenue − cost = 55,000 − 40,000 = ₹15,000.
quiz.mistake: Adds cost and revenue

quiz.q: A volunteer finds that 18 of 60 shops charged above MRP for bottled water. What percentage overcharged?
quiz.mistake: Reports the count as a percentage

quiz.q: Which of these is a suitable project on social welfare?
options: Immunisation coverage of children in a village
quiz.explain: It is a local welfare issue that can be studied with a survey.
quiz.mistake: Picks a topic far from local data collection

quiz.q: A survey of 80 school-age children in a slum finds 12 have dropped out. What is the dropout rate?
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Role-based projects still follow the standard steps of a statistical study.
Reason (R): Every project needs a problem, data, analysis and conclusions, whatever role the student plays.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The role sets the context; the method stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks role-play replaces method

quiz.q: Which data would best help a project on household saving habits?
options: Monthly income, monthly saving and where savings are kept
quiz.explain: These variables directly describe saving behaviour.
quiz.mistake: Collects irrelevant data

teach.ask: Gappu is playing 'drinking water officer' for his forest. 'What should my project study, and how?'
teach.praise: Tweet! I'll survey households on water availability and quality, analyse it, and suggest improvements!
teach.nudge: Good! What exactly will you measure about the water? And whom will you ask?

topics.title: A consumer survey: questionnaire and presentation

learn.hook: Which toothpaste do families in your colony use, and why? A consumer survey answers this the way real marketing teams do.
points: A consumer survey questionnaire covers: demographic details (age, sex, family size), income and occupation, brand used, satisfaction, preferences (taste, ingredients, price) and media that influenced the choice.

Present the age distribution of respondents with a table and a bar diagram. Family size and spending can be grouped into classes and shown with suitable diagrams: a bar diagram for counts of a discrete variable, a histogram for continuous classes.
Make a frequency distribution of income or monthly spending and find the mean, using the assumed mean or step deviation method to simplify arithmetic.
Show occupational status of respondents with a pie diagram; tabulate brand preferences and the reasons for choice as counts or percentages.

example.q: In a survey of 120 respondents, 48 are salaried, 36 self-employed, 24 students and 12 retired. Find the pie angles.

learn.reallife: FMCG companies like those selling toothpaste and soaps run such consumer surveys across Indian towns before launching new variants.

games.title: Match the data to the presentation
pairs: Age groups of respondents with counts

quiz.q: Which of these is a demographic question in a consumer survey?
options: Which toothpaste brand do you use?
How satisfied are you with the brand?
quiz.explain: Age is a demographic characteristic of the respondent.
quiz.mistake: Confuses demographic questions with brand questions

quiz.q: Out of 200 respondents, 70 use Brand X. What percentage use Brand X?
quiz.mistake: Reports the count as a percentage

quiz.q: Occupational status of respondents is best shown by a:
quiz.explain: Categories that make up a whole suit a pie diagram.
quiz.mistake: Uses a time-series graph for categories

quiz.q: In a pie chart of 120 respondents, the sector for students is 72°. How many respondents are students?
quiz.mistake: Reads the angle as the count

quiz.q: Monthly spending classes ₹300–500, ₹500–700, ₹700–900 have frequencies 10, 25, 15. Find the mean spending.
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle class's mid-point (₹600) as the mean, ignoring frequencies

quiz.q: Monthly spending of respondents is grouped into continuous classes ₹0–500, ₹500–1,000, ₹1,000–1,500. Which diagram suits it best?
quiz.explain: A frequency distribution with continuous classes is shown by adjacent rectangles: a histogram.
quiz.mistake: Uses a pie or line graph for a continuous frequency distribution

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A consumer survey questionnaire should ask about media that influenced the purchase.
Reason (R): Such information helps the company judge which advertising channels work.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Knowing media influence helps companies plan advertising.
quiz.mistake: Thinks media questions are irrelevant

quiz.q: Using A = 600 and c = 200, Σfd′ = 10 and Σf = 50 for monthly spending, the mean is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by c

teach.ask: Gappu is surveying which seed brand birds prefer. 'What should my questionnaire ask, and how do I show the answers?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Ask about the bird, its income, brand, satisfaction and media, then show it with tables, bars and pies!
teach.nudge: Good! What personal details and brand details would you ask? How will you present the answers?

topics.title: Interpreting results and writing the conclusion

learn.hook: Your survey shows 60% of users like Brand A, but only 30% are 'very satisfied'. What does that mean for the company? Interpretation turns numbers into insight.
points: Interpret satisfaction by brand: compare the share of 'satisfied' users across brands, not just the number of users.
Interpret preferences: e.g. if most respondents prefer herbal ingredients, products with such ingredients may gain share.
Interpret media influence: identify which medium (TV, social media, newspapers, word of mouth) influenced most buyers.
The concluding note summarises the main findings, states their limits (sample size, area covered) and gives practical suggestions.

example.q: Brand A has 80 users, of whom 40 are very satisfied; Brand B has 40 users, of whom 30 are very satisfied. Which brand satisfies its users better?
steps: Brand B has fewer users but a higher satisfaction rate.

learn.reallife: Market research firms tell clients both 'reach' (how many use the product) and 'satisfaction rate' (how happy users are), because the two can differ.

games.title: Interpreting survey results
items: The brand with more users must have more satisfied users in percentage terms.
Satisfaction rates must be compared, not raw counts.
A concluding note should mention the limitations of the survey.
E.g. small sample or limited area.
If most buyers learnt about a product on social media, that medium matters for advertising.
That is the interpretation of media influence.
Conclusions should go beyond what the data show.
Conclusions must be supported by the findings.
Comparing percentages helps when groups are of different sizes.

games.title: Writing a concluding note
items: Mention the limitations of the study

quiz.q: Brand A: 80 users, 40 very satisfied. Brand B: 40 users, 30 very satisfied. What percentage of Brand B's users are very satisfied?
quiz.mistake: Uses the total sample instead of Brand B's users

quiz.q: In the same data (A: 40 of 80, B: 30 of 40 very satisfied), which conclusion is correct?
options: Brand A satisfies its users better because it has more satisfied users
Brand B satisfies its users better because its satisfaction rate is higher
quiz.explain: 75% for B versus 50% for A.
quiz.mistake: Compares raw counts instead of rates

quiz.q: Out of 150 respondents, 90 say TV advertisements influenced their choice. What percentage is this?
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong denominator

quiz.q: A concluding note of a project should include:
quiz.explain: It summarises results, admits limits and suggests action.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a conclusion just repeats the data

quiz.q: A survey of only 30 households in one street concludes about the whole city. What is the main limitation?
options: The sample may not represent the city
quiz.explain: A tiny sample from one street may not reflect the whole city.
quiz.mistake: Ignores representativeness

quiz.q: 72 of 120 respondents prefer toothpaste with herbal ingredients. What fraction is this?
quiz.mistake: Divides 120 by 72

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Interpretation of data should be supported by the findings.
Reason (R): Unsupported conclusions can mislead decision makers.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Conclusions that go beyond the evidence can lead to wrong decisions.
quiz.mistake: Treats interpretation as personal opinion

quiz.q: Which is the best suggestion from a finding that most young buyers were influenced by social media?
options: Spend more of the advertising budget on social media aimed at young buyers
quiz.explain: The suggestion follows directly from the finding.
quiz.mistake: Suggests action unrelated to the finding

teach.ask: Gappu's survey shows 70 birds use Brand A seeds but only 20 love them, while 30 use Brand B and 25 love them. 'Which brand is better?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Brand A: 20/70 ≈ 29%, Brand B: 25/30 ≈ 83%. Brand B wins on satisfaction, so compare rates, not counts!
teach.nudge: Hmm, is it fair to compare 20 and 25 directly when the brands have different numbers of users? What should we compare?
